blood-atlas.title: The Blood Atlas
blood-atlas.lede: What is your blood telling you?
blood-atlas.blurb: An open-source GoInvo prototype that maps more than 6,000 blood tests to body systems and everyday concerns. Suchi Sundarraman and I made it for people with lab results in hand.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.heading: Lab results arrive with little context.

blocks.text: Standard lab tests can miss the personal factors that shape care.
Looking up a result on your own gives too much information or too little.
A routine panel measures fewer than 30 of the 6,000+ blood tests in our catalogue.
Most of what blood can tell you is never looked at, and people can’t easily see that.

sections.label: My Role
sections.heading: A GoInvo project, made with Suchi.

blocks.text: Made with Suchi Sundarraman as an open-source GoInvo project.
I designed and built the prototype, including the data pipeline and the map, database and upload views.
July to September 2026, from a symptom explorer and a step-by-step wizard to today’s map.

sections.label: The Data
sections.heading: Building the catalogue first.

blocks.text: We started from LOINC, the standard code system for lab tests, and turned it into one data file.
Every test is tagged by body system, by who it’s for (children, pregnancy, age-based screening) and by concerns like fatigue or hair loss.
Only about 200 descriptions are quoted from a named authority such as MedlinePlus, with a link.
The rest are written from LOINC data, and labelled that way.

figures.alt: The Blood Atlas database: tests with their system, what they are used for, who they come up for and a source link
figures.caption: The database, with quoted descriptions marked and linked

sections.label: The Design
sections.heading: From a list of tests to a map.

blocks.text: Early versions worked like a search: pick a concern, get a list of tests.
That couldn’t say what a pattern of results might mean.
Now the Atlas starts from results you already have.
The map reads left to right: routine panel markers, the concerns they point to, and follow-up tests.
Mark a result low or high to see what it could point to, including things your panel couldn’t measure.
Upload a lab PDF, such as one from MyChart. It’s read on your device and never sent anywhere.

figures.alt: The Blood Atlas map: routine panel markers on the left, personal concerns in the middle, follow-up tests on the right
figures.caption: The map: your panel, the concerns it points to, and what would follow up

sections.label: Outcomes
sections.heading: An open map of blood testing.

blocks.text: Live as an open-source prototype.
It doesn’t diagnose, recommend tests or know your history, and it says so.
The bigger idea: weigh symptoms, history, medications, trends and wearable data to help people know what to ask a clinician.

sections.label: What I Learned
sections.heading: Showing what we don’t know.

blocks.text: Most of what blood can measure is never measured, and most of our catalogue isn’t yet source-quoted. Saying both openly built trust.
Next: a condition layer linking a diagnosis like iron-deficiency anemia to its symptoms, markers and a screen-then-confirm path.

guidelines.title: Guidelines.com
guidelines.lede: AI answers that show their evidence
guidelines.blurb: Design lead on an AI answer engine for a library 1M+ clinicians use each year. I set the rules for answers when evidence is weak, conflicting or missing, and prototyped every case.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.heading: Five libraries, one clinician’s question.

blocks.text: 3,000+ guidelines from 50+ medical societies, 7,120 drugs, 580K clinical trials and 14.6M PubMed abstracts.
Each lived in its own section with its own search, so clinicians connected the evidence themselves.
The client wanted AI answers, without risking 20 years of clinical trust.

sections.label: My Role
sections.heading: Design lead, from research hub to prototypes.

blocks.text: I led design at GoInvo, working with Eric Benoit, April to June 2026.
I built the client’s deliverables site: research, interviews, a feature plan and every prototype in one place.
I designed and built the answer, browse, monograph, library and chat prototypes.

sections.label: Research
sections.heading: Fast or trustworthy. Clinicians needed both.

blocks.text: I compared 7 AI clinical tools, including OpenEvidence, UpToDate Expert AI and ClinicalKey AI, on users, strengths, gaps and price.
The fast ones weren’t guideline sources. The authoritative ones were slow, cluttered or offered no follow-up questions.
Three clinician interviews showed the cost: they feared AI inventing citations, so they checked every reference by hand.
A site inventory and a 16-area feature plan ranked what to build first.

sections.label: Rules First
sections.heading: Eight ways an answer can go.

blocks.text: Before settling the chat, I designed how an answer behaves in 8 scenarios: strong, weak, conflicting, from a trial, or no match.
When two societies disagree, the answer shows both instead of picking one.
A confidence score weighs relevance, authority, content and recency, and shows all four.
I built it as an interface around the interface: toggles switch each part of the answer on or off, live in sessions with clinicians.

sections.label: One Search
sections.heading: All the evidence, one search.

blocks.text: One search bar and combinable filters replace four tabs with a dropdown each.
Browse stays next to the AI answer, for clinicians who already know the guideline.
Drug monographs open with key facts, an outline and a link to the original.
Mobile is its own product: an assistant that opens on common tasks.

figures.alt: Guidelines browse page with a single search bar and a multi-select specialty filter
figures.caption: Browse: one search bar and filters that combine

figures.alt: Drug monograph page with a key-facts summary and an outline of sections
figures.caption: Drug monograph: key facts first, every section one click away

figures.alt: Mobile assistant prototype for clinicians with suggested tasks and a message box
figures.caption: Mobile assistant prototype

sections.label: Outcomes
sections.heading: From prototypes to the live product.

blocks.text: The client built the design in over time, and Guidelines.com now answers clinical questions in plain language.
Every claim cites the exact section, with its recommendation class and evidence level, as the scenarios tool set out.
One answer draws on guidelines, drug monographs and trials together, each labeled by type.
The Android app is live, with iOS on the way.
Clinicians trust an answer they can check. Showing the client every case side by side, instead of one polished screen, got us to that decision faster.

figures.alt: The live Guidelines.com: a clinical question answered with numbered citations, a source card showing guideline section 5.4.3, Class 2a and Level A evidence
figures.caption: The live Guidelines.com, Nov 2026: every claim opens its source

ipsos-flow.title: Ipsos Flow
ipsos-flow.blurb: I led design for two years on Ipsos Flow: one platform to replace 15 tools across 50+ countries, for projects from $1M to $40M.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.heading: 15 tools, and the real record lived in Excel.

blocks.text: Ipsos grew by buying companies, so 15 tools were in use and every country and team worked its own way.
The same thing had different names in different systems, and Excel was the real system of record.
Nothing carried a project from one stage to the next.
Details were re-entered, or lost, every time a project changed hands.

sections.label: My Role
sections.heading: A design team of two.

blocks.text: GoInvo’s design team was two people: the project lead and me.
I owned the design system, the visual and interaction direction, and consistency across pods.
Concepts from others came through me to become final deliverables, annotated with system rules for developers.
In dev audits, the project lead wrote tickets while I fixed UI issues on the spot.
I mentored the designers who joined and left along the way.
I remembered every decision and kept the design consistent through two years of changing scope.

sections.label: How I Started
sections.heading: Mapping how work got done first.

blocks.text: I mapped how work got done through client demos, sessions with each role, document reviews and talks with power users.
The map showed an 8-stage, 152-step workflow full of duplicated work and broken handoffs.
The workarounds had become the workflow.
The main goal: cut the duplication and keep the whole project lifecycle in one place.

figures.alt: Interactive map of the 8-stage Ipsos workflow
figures.caption: The current workflow, 8 stages and 152 steps (interactive)

sections.label: Designing Through Ambiguity
sections.heading: The data model took two years.

blocks.text: When engineering split into parallel pods, I rewrote the system rules so each pod could work alone without drifting.
I worked directly with each pod owner, and added annotations and prototypes so new teams could catch up.
The harder problem was the data model. Every major stakeholder had a strong, reasonable view of it.
Getting it wrong meant political tension, slower workflows and lost revenue.
We concept-tested competing data models and workflows as clickable prototypes in client demos, so people could click through an idea instead of arguing in the abstract.
Each round went back to finance, operations and regional leads, and the next version answered their pushback.
Nobody set the MVP’s data model up front. We worked it out together over two years.

sections.label: The Hard Work
sections.heading: Many stakeholders, no single owner.

blocks.text: No one had the authority to make 50+ countries adopt a new tool.
Decisions were spread across finance, operations, research, regional markets and engineering, up to COO and CTO level.
In the Execution pod alone, the average design decision was redirected more than 50 times before it stuck.
One long debate: how closely to tie financial data (budgets, revenue, costs) to execution data (fieldwork, deliverables, timelines).
Tying them closely helped teams coordinate, but caused ownership tension between finance and operations.
We settled on a shared operational data layer with role-based visibility.
I designed how budgets, revenue and costs sit beside fieldwork and deliverables on one project, with finance and operations each seeing what they own.
People doubted software could handle the edge cases that had built up in spreadsheets for years.

sections.label: Key Components
sections.heading: How three key screens changed.

blocks.text: These are data-dense screens: one project carries finance, staffing, fieldwork and deliverables data.
I kept them scannable with a clear hierarchy, item-type headers and one continuous view of the whole project lifecycle.
From cluttered to easy to scan.
The sidebar changed in style, hierarchy and structure as we learned what people needed at a glance.
Most changes came from the shifting data model, pod owners, stakeholders and client demos.
We pushed for user research from the start, but the client kept saying no.
From a bold concept to a practical panel layout.
The first concept was ambitious and visual, made in a blind sprint before we could see all 15 tools.
Once we knew the full scope, we landed on a panel layout with a continuous tree view: a whole project lifecycle on one screen.
Familiar to researchers, usable by coders.
The questionnaire designer is an inline editor modeled on the word processors researchers already use.
It has built-in guidance for writing questions, and formats that work for coders and researchers.
Previews and translations happen in the editor, not as later steps.
We pushed for an AI layer early. Parts were added once the client came around.

sections.label: Outcomes
sections.heading: A working platform, piloted in 2026.

blocks.text: Interactive prototypes were how we tested workflow ideas, lowered the risk of architecture decisions and kept the client aligned.
They became production-ready screens for an MVP pilot in one of Ipsos’s most complex service lines.
The pilot put the whole workflow in one place and brought finance, staffing and delivery data together.
Built and piloted in February 2026. Development is paused after a leadership change and reorganization.

figures.alt: Flow MVP pilot — live platform screenshot, February 2026
figures.caption: The MVP pilot, February 2026

sections.label: What I Learned
sections.heading: The hardest problems weren’t on screen.

blocks.text: Designing an enterprise platform is mostly about alignment and abstraction. The hardest work on this project was agreeing on shared definitions, sorting out who owned what across a spread-out company, and balancing company-wide consistency with local autonomy.
Beyond the design system, the most valuable thing I helped build was a shared operational model that teams in dozens of countries could trust and build on.

prism.title: PRISM
prism.lede: A second opinion for health handouts
prism.blurb: A free, open-source tool that checks patient materials against 23 published frameworks. Sonia Seto and I made it for designers who want feedback based on evidence, not opinion.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.heading: “This looks great” isn’t feedback.

blocks.text: People who design patient materials often hear “this looks great” at handoff, and then nothing.
Published score sheets exist, like the CDC Clear Communication Index and AHRQ’s PEMAT.
Each one is a separate checklist of 20+ items to work through by hand.
We wanted to check a piece against evidence, before and after it goes out.

sections.label: My Role
sections.heading: Made by two designers.

blocks.text: Made with Sonia Seto of Sonia Seto Studios.
I designed the tool and built the prototype, with Claude helping write and test the code.
I kept a running log of every change and why.
July to October 2026, and still in progress.

sections.label: The Rule
sections.heading: It can grade the work, but never write it.

blocks.text: One rule: PRISM scores a draft, but nothing it writes ever reaches a patient.
It checks against published instruments such as the CDC Clear Communication Index, PEMAT, SAM, DISCERN and IPDAS.
Only frameworks from a fixed list can be used.
Every score quotes the part of the document it’s based on and links to its source.
What the tool can’t measure is left for the person to rate. Unrated items don’t count as a pass.

figures.alt: The Framework Compass page listing published frameworks with links to their sources
figures.caption: The Framework Compass: 23 frameworks, each linked to its source

sections.label: The Design
sections.heading: A proofing desk for patient handouts.

blocks.text: It feels like a proofing desk: the draft on a sheet of paper, the checks as score-sheet rows.
The one bright colour is highlighter yellow, for flagged words.
Four steps: set a brief, add a draft (type, paste, or upload a Word file, PDF or image), pick frameworks, review scores.
For “25%” it suggests “1 in 4” and names the research behind it.
Everything stays in the browser. Nothing is uploaded.

figures.alt: The PRISM studio with a material panel, a brief, framework picker and four getting-started steps
figures.caption: The studio, ready for a draft

sections.label: Outcomes
sections.heading: Free, open source and live.

blocks.text: Live as a free, open-source prototype.
Checks drafts against 23 frameworks across clarity, interaction, behaviour and outcomes.
An AI evaluator, bound by the same rules, is built and tested but not yet connected.
Try PRISM ↗ See it as a talk →

sections.label: What I Learned
sections.heading: Where to let the model in.

blocks.text: Deciding what the AI could do mattered more than any feature.
We let a model write copy, name criteria and write citations, then cut all three. Each made the scores harder to trust.
A tool earns trust by showing its evidence, and by saying so when there isn’t enough.

prolaio.title: Prolaio
prolaio.lede: Engaging people within a trial’s rules
prolaio.blurb: A heart study app, run in 90-day cycles, that can’t reward engagement or interpret health data. In five weeks we went from 7 interviews to one clinical app covering 38 moments.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.heading: What people want most, the app can’t offer.

blocks.text: Prolaio runs at-home heart studies in 90-day cycles: a patch, a bracelet, daily readings and questionnaires, all through one app.
People were leaving before the data came in, and Prolaio wants them back for the next cycle, and the one after.
All 7 people we interviewed take part for the pay or to learn about their own health.
Legally, the app can’t offer either. It can’t reward engaging, and interpreting someone’s data would turn a study into marketing.
So engagement had to come from somewhere else.

sections.label: My Role
sections.heading: From the interview guide to the prototype.

blocks.text: Designer at GoInvo, with Claire Lin (lead) and Juhan Sonin (advisor).
I wrote the interview guide, screener and questionnaire, building on Prolaio’s earlier guide with Claude.
I helped moderate, took notes and built the interview reports.
I turned the concepts into one working prototype, built with Claude.

sections.label: What We Heard
sections.heading: Facts, not verdicts. Clinical, not playful.

blocks.text: Your guess: which look would people want every day in a heart study?
Seven moderated remote sessions in September, with people aged 36 to 71 who manage chronic conditions.
A game-like look read as low stakes. One participant said it made him question a past study’s sponsor.
6 of 7 had lost trust in a past study through a failure, like a device that stopped syncing unnoticed.
So the app gives facts without verdicts: plain definitions, ranges, people’s own trends, and daily proof their data arrived.
The look is clinical first. Streaks and trivia arrive on day 3, quiet and optional.

sections.label: One App
sections.heading: 40 concepts, one participant’s 90 days.

blocks.text: The concepts grew from 21 to 40 over two rounds of review with Prolaio.
I placed each one where it belongs in a participant’s study, and merged or cut the rest.
The result is one app across 38 moments, from opening the kit to the end of a cycle.
11 of the moments are “what ifs”, because people quit when things go wrong:

The bracelet won’t connectThe bracelet stopped syncingThe cuff was too looseThe patch feels itchySetup wasn’t finishedBack after a breakNothing is due todayTasks in any orderThe consent changedThe study endsA year in

sections.label: Two Axes
sections.heading: When in the study, where in the app.

blocks.text: The prototype shows the app on two axes: the study’s timeline across the top, the app’s structure down the side.
Pick any day, from setup to two years in, and see what a participant sees, with features unlocking on their day.
In reviews, Prolaio could ask what happens on day 30 and see it, instead of reading about it.
Like the rest of the project’s deliverables, it’s a self-contained site built with Claude.

figures.alt: The Prolaio prototype: the study timeline across the top, the app map on the left, the phone in the middle and the features that unlock over time on the right

sections.label: Outcomes
sections.heading: Five weeks, ready for testing.

blocks.text: Sep7 interviews
1 Oct21 concepts
6 Oct40 concepts
19 OctOne app
30 OctTestable prototype
From interviews to a prototype people can test in about five weeks, through four versions.
Next: usability testing with study participants, then keeping people for 180 and 360 days.
Start the hardest part first. Recruiting people with chronic conditions takes time, so the screener and guide should be ready on day one.
And people stay when the basics work, before any motivation feature.

waipo.title: Waipo?
waipo.blurb: A 20-page graphic memoir about Alzheimer’s disease across three generations, made as a graduate project from family memories and medical research.

sections.label: The Story
sections.heading: A family story, told out loud.

blocks.text: When my grandmother, Waipo, was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, our family didn’t talk about it openly. It was a slow, confusing loss that my mom carried mostly on her own, while I watched from a distance and moved further away with every new city.

This comic is my attempt to close that distance. It started with conversations with my mom, the kind we’d never really had before, about memory, fear, genetics and what we could do. I added what I learned from the research: Alzheimer’s isn’t inevitable, and four everyday habits can lower the risk.
I didn’t want to make a medical explainer. I wanted to make something honest that shows how messy a diagnosis is, how worry passes down a family, and the small, practical reasons to stay hopeful.
Help people understand how common Alzheimer’s is, and show a calm, open way to respond to a frightening diagnosis, because it’s not the end of the world.
The general public, and especially families going through the same thing: people dealing with a parent’s or grandparent’s diagnosis while wondering about their own risk.

sections.label: Story Outline
sections.heading: The story, page by page.

steps: Drifting boats, a picture of memory coming loose.
A close moment with Waipo, and what there was to lose.
Boarding school, exchanges, then Canada, each move taking me further away.
The diagnosis arrives, and the distance suddenly feels different.
Neurons, synapses, amyloid beta and risk factors, explained through analogies and drawings.
Graduate, home for Chinese New Year
Coming home and seeing Waipo differently. She is there, but somewhere else.
Small, tender moments from her daily routine.
She no longer remembers, and there is grief in being forgotten by someone who loves you.
Concern for the family · Dialog with mom
The risk factors become personal, and my mom and I talk openly about our worries and what we can do.
Four habits backed by research, New Year’s fireworks, a family photo, and a choice to stay hopeful.

sections.label: Production
sections.heading: Rough, line, colour.

blocks.text: Every page went through the same three stages: loose sketches, clean line art, then full colour. Splitting it up let me solve one thing at a time, first the idea, then the form, then the feeling.
Teal, warm salmon and cream felt personal without being sentimental. Keeping to three colours makes every scene, from a childhood memory to a diagram of the brain, feel like part of the same story.

sections.label: Read the Comic
sections.heading: Read the comic.

sections.label: Reflection
sections.heading: What making it taught me.

blocks.text: A comic can do things a pamphlet or infographic can’t. It can stay with uncertainty and grief and still give people useful information. Public health rarely uses the form, and this project convinced me comics are a serious way to communicate about health.

Writing about my own family showed me that the more specific a story is, the more people recognize themselves in it. The more exactly I drew the way my grandmother sat on the sofa, the more readers saw their own grandmothers.
